article_sentences: Climate change increased the damage caused by the tropical Cyclone Arnab, which struck eastern India on October 28, by 33%, resulting in tens of millions of dollars in additional direct economic losses compared to a pre-industrial climate baseline, according to a new study.
It added that the storm brought intense rain, peak 1-minute sustained winds of up to 202 kilometres per hour, and severe damage to infrastructure across Andhra Pradesh.
The study was carried out by researchers at the Imperial College London’s Grantham Institute and published on Thursday (November 5, 2026).

For their analysis, researchers used the Imperial College Storm Model (IRIS) to simulate Cyclone Arnab under current conditions (plus 1.3° Celsius above pre-industrial levels) versus a counterfactual climate without human-induced warming.
“Climate change increased Cyclone Arnab’s maximum wind speed by approximately 5%, and intensified its eyewall rainfall rate by 11% at landfall,” according to the study.

It also revealed that direct damage to physical assets in India was estimated to be 33% higher than it would have been in a pre-industrial climate baseline, attributing roughly 25% of the total economic damage directly to climate change.
In a statement, Dr. Nathan Sparks, researcher at the Department of Physics, Imperial College London, said: “These findings are a powerful reminder of the price of inaction.
The costs of climate change are not hypothetical future projections — they are hitting coastal communities in eastern India today.”

stories.headline: How 3D Visual Models Can Make Flood Preparedness Training More Practical in Assam
stories.title: How 3D Visual Models Can Make Flood Preparedness Training More Practical in Assam
stories.summary: Flood preparedness is difficult to teach through instructions alone. A resident may understand a warning in principle but still struggle to picture how rising water could affect the road to a shelter, where medicines should be stored or why one household may need more time to evacuate than another. In Assam, where floods repeatedly disrupt homes, transport and education, preparedness activities need to turn general advice into decisions people can recognise. Simple 3D visual models can support that process by giving students and community members something concrete to examine, question and rearrange. An AI 3D generator can help educators create initial models of objects such as raised houses, relief boats, emergency supply boxes and temporary shelters from written descriptions. Meshy works through a browser and can export generated assets for further editing. The free plan is enough to generate and preview models; downloading them requires a paid plan. These models can support lesson planning and tabletop exercises, but they must not be treated as official maps, engineering designs or predictions of how a real flood will develop. Why Visual Preparedness Exercises Can Help Conventional awareness materials often use posters, maps and lists of instructions. These remain valuable, especially because they are inexpensive to distribute and easy to print. However, they may not show how several decisions are connected. A tabletop scene can make those relationships easier to discuss. Participants might see a cluster of houses, a school on higher ground, a blocked road, a boat landing point and a temporary shelter. The facilitator can then introduce a scenario: heavy rainfall has continued, an official warning has been issued and one route is no longer usable. The group must decide what information it needs, which official instructions to follow and who may require additional assistance. The model does not provide the answer. It creates a shared setting in which people can explain their reasoning. Make the Scenario Local Without Pretending It Is Exact A training model can reflect familiar features such as stilted homes, village roads, embankments, livestock areas or elevated community buildings. Familiarity makes the exercise easier to understand, but the scene should be clearly labelled as illustrative. Using the name of a real village while inventing roads, water depths or shelter locations could cause confusion. If a session refers to actual geography, the relevant information must come from authorised maps and local disaster-management officials. Build the Exercise Around People, Not Objects A preparedness model becomes more useful when participants consider the needs of different residents. A household with young children faces different constraints from one caring for an older person who has limited mobility. Someone who depends on refrigerated medicine may require a plan for maintaining safe storage. Families with livestock also need instructions appropriate to local arrangements. One possible classroom or community exercise could proceed as follows: • Introduce an imaginary settlement and explain that it is not an official risk map. • Assign participants different household situations. • Present an official warning and close one route in the scenario. • Ask each group what information, supplies and assistance it would need. • Compare the decisions with guidance provided by trained facilitators. • Record questions that should be referred to local authorities. • End by identifying the difference between a classroom scenario and a real emergency. This format encourages participation without asking students or untrained residents to make operational decisions beyond their responsibility. Include Communication Breakdowns Flood exercises should not assume that every participant has continuous internet access, a charged phone or the same level of literacy. The facilitator can introduce a power cut, weak mobile coverage or a message available in only one language. Participants can then discuss how verified information might reach households through several channels. The exercise should reinforce the use of official warnings and recognised local communication networks rather than encouraging people to rely on an unverified social media post. Connect Visual Activities to Official Preparedness Guidance The National Disaster Management Authority's community-based disaster risk reduction guidelines frame communities as active participants in preparedness, response, recovery and risk reduction. A 3D exercise can support this approach when it helps residents identify questions, understand responsibilities and practise communication. It cannot replace official hazard assessments, evacuation planning or emergency drills. Water movement depends on rainfall, river conditions, terrain, drainage and infrastructure. A generated visual scene does not calculate any of these factors. The safest approach is to use the model as a discussion aid within a programme led or reviewed by qualified teachers, disaster-management personnel and local authorities. Review Every Model Before It Enters the Classroom AI-generated assets can contain plausible-looking errors. A boat may have an unrealistic hull, a staircase may be unusable, or a shelter may appear structurally sound despite being only a visual interpretation. Before an exercise, the facilitator should inspect the models for misleading details. Objects should be simplified when realism could imply engineering accuracy. Labels, colours and symbols also need review so that they do not conflict with official materials. Separate Visualisation from Engineering A generated model of a raised house may help explain why people protect documents and supplies above expected water levels. It cannot determine the safe height of a real building or verify its foundation. Likewise, a model of a rescue boat may support a discussion about boarding order and essential supplies, but it cannot establish capacity, stability or operational suitability. Those questions require approved equipment specifications and trained personnel. This distinction should be stated at the beginning and end of every exercise. Design for Schools and Low-Resource Settings A useful preparedness activity should not depend on advanced computers. The models can be shown as still images, short rotations or simple videos if an interactive viewer is impractical. Where 3D printing is available, a few durable objects may be printed for repeated classroom use, but printing is optional. Facilitators should also provide text descriptions and high-contrast diagrams. Students with visual, motor or cognitive disabilities may need tactile elements, additional explanation or alternative ways to participate. Language matters as well. Instructions should use terms understood by the intended community, with translations reviewed by local speakers. A technically correct message can still fail if it is unfamiliar, ambiguous or difficult to read. Measure Learning Through Decisions and Questions The quality of an exercise should not be judged by how realistic its models look. A visually polished scene has limited value if participants leave without knowing where official warnings come from or whom to contact. A better evaluation asks whether participants can distinguish verified information from rumours, identify household members who may need assistance, explain why an evacuation order must be followed and name questions that require an official answer. Teachers can repeat the same scenario later with one condition changed. A route may close earlier, the shelter may become unavailable or communication may fail. Comparing the group's responses can reveal whether participants are applying principles rather than memorising one sequence. Frequently Asked Questions Can AI-generated 3D models predict which areas will flood? No. They are visual assets, not hydrological models. Flood forecasts and risk maps must come from authorised agencies using validated data and appropriate scientific methods. Should students design real evacuation routes with these models? Students may discuss hypothetical choices for learning purposes, but actual evacuation routes and shelter locations must be determined and communicated by responsible authorities. Is 3D printing required for this type of activity? No. Models can be displayed on a screen or converted into still images. The teaching objective should determine the format, particularly where devices, electricity or internet access are limited. Use Technology to Strengthen Preparedness Conversations 3D visualisation can make flood-preparedness training more participatory, particularly when abstract instructions are placed within a recognisable scenario. It can help students ask better questions and help facilitators identify misunderstandings before an emergency. Its role must remain carefully defined. Meshy can accelerate the creation of visual assets for a lesson, while local knowledge, official guidance and trained professionals determine what the exercise should teach. The most effective model is therefore not necessarily the most detailed one. It is the model that encourages people to discuss realistic needs, recognise the limits of their information and understand where to obtain trusted instructions when conditions become dangerous. Could a Democratic-controlled Congress investigate Musk's government contracts and business interests? Will he spend even more ahead of the 2028 presidential elections? stories.headline: Jaipur celebrates Pia Dandia's election to US House of Representatives from Florida
stories.title: Jaipur celebrates Pia Dandia's election to US House of Representatives from Florida
stories.summary: Indian-American Democrat, whose family hails from Jaipur, defeated Republican Casey Askar
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The festive season is witnessing an added celebration in Jaipur's Dandia household after Indian-American Democrat Pia Dandia won election to the US House of Representatives from Florida, defeating Republican candidate Casey Askar in a constituency traditionally dominated by Republicans.
Dandia's victory drew congratulations from Indian-American Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal, who welcomed her as the third South Asian American woman in the House, alongside herself and Aisha Wahab.
"Congratulations to @PiaforCongress for winning her election!
I am so excited to welcome the third South Asian American woman (along with me and @aishabbwahab) to the House!!!" Jayapal wrote on X.
Although born and raised in the United States, Dandia has maintained close links with Jaipur and India since childhood.
Her family gathered at their home near Rambagh Circle Road in Jaipur to celebrate her election.
Dandia is the daughter of Dr Rohit Dandia and Bharati Dandia, and the granddaughter of Dr P C Dandia, a distinguished pharmacologist who is 101 years old.
Dr P C Dandia served as professor emeritus at Sawai Man Singh Medical College in Jaipur, where his son also studied medicine.
Her paternal grandmother, Dr Chandrakanta Dandia, was director of the Department of Adult Education at Rajasthan University.
Her parents moved to the United States around four decades ago.
Dandia grew up with strong connections to her Indian heritage.
Her parents sent her on trips to India as a child to spend time with her cousins in Jaipur.

stories.headline: White House sticks to Trump agenda after midterm election outcome
stories.title: White House sticks to Trump agenda after midterm election outcome
stories.summary: Washington, Nov 5 : The White House has vowed to resist attempts to reverse President Donald Trump's policies during the final two years of his presidency, predicting that Democratic challenges on immigration, taxation, energy and other issues would fail. The White House Office on Wednesday (local time) defended the administration's record and raised the prospect of another impeachment effort, while offering no details of a specific proceeding or legislative proposal. "In the final two years of his presidency, Democrats will try -- and fail -- to reverse everything President Trump has done," the statement said. The release, issued a day after the November 3 midterm elections, portrayed the coming political contest as a defence of Trump's existing policies. It did not announce a new executive action, legislative initiative or negotiating position. "These efforts will fail; the American people have already rejected this agenda," the White House said. The statement placed immigration enforcement prominently among the policies it pledged to defend. It accused Democrats of seeking to undo border restrictions and large-scale deportations, presenting those predictions as part of a broader attack on the opposition. It did not identify specific Democratic bills or statements supporting each of the intentions it attributed to the party. Its descriptions of what Democrats would pursue were the administration's political assertions, rather than an agreed account of the opposition's programme. On the economy, the White House defended Trump's tax cuts and claimed they had delivered record growth. It also credited the administration with record energy production and what it described as American energy independence. The release did not provide figures, time periods or comparisons to substantiate those economic and energy claims. It linked to a separate White House account of Trump's second-term record. Law enforcement was another focus. The statement claimed that Trump had produced the largest decline in violent crime in modern history, but did not include supporting crime statistics or specify the period covered by that comparison. The White House also pledged to defend its actions against diversity, equity and inclusion programmes, commonly known as DEI. It accused Democrats of seeking to restore those programmes and reverse administration policies affecting transgender minors. Other passages alleged that Democrats would rebuild censorship mechanisms and weaken efforts to curb waste, fraud and abuse. The statement did not identify particular measures underpinning those accusations. The White House accused Democrats of wanting to expand the Supreme Court and predicted another attempt to impeach Trump. It did not name lawmakers pursuing those steps or describe a formal proposal. The release characterised the President's earlier impeachment proceedings as failed efforts and said future attempts to reverse his agenda would meet the same outcome. The message was a pledge of continued political resistance: "President Trump will never stop fighting." --IANS

stories.headline: Salman faces backlash over 'Teri Sexy Beauty' song in Maatrubhumi
stories.title: Salman faces backlash over 'Teri Sexy Beauty' song in Maatrubhumi
stories.summary: Mumbai, Nov 5 : Bollywood superstar Salman Khan has found himself at the receiving end of severe criticism on social media after unveiling his latest song, ‘Teri Sexy Beauty’, from his upcoming film Maatrubhumi: May War Rest in Peace. While the actor's return to playback singing after 11 years has grabbed attention, the song has left a section of netizens baffled. Many questioned its relevance in a film based on the 2020 Galwan Valley clash between Indian and Chinese troops. The song, featuring Salman Khan and Chitrangda Singh, was released in the early hours of November 4. Salman also shared a video announcing the track on social media with a rather cheeky caption. "Departure time 5:12 am…. Flight on time , 2 pegs down taking off with my sexy beauty… pata nahi kahaan mai land karoon #TeriSexyBeauty Out Now" The song features Salman crooning alongside Muskaan, with additional vocals by Sajid Khan. It shows Chitrangada Singh in a red saree with Salman also dancing, and the both sharing some romantic and flirtation moments along with a couple of drinks. The song's lyrics and picturisation have not gone down well with a section of the audience, particularly considering the sensitivity of the film's subject. Soon after its release, several X users questioned how a song with lyrics such as "Teri sexy beauty ka fan ban gaya hoon, main do peg pee ke aeroplane ban gaya hoon" could feature in a patriotic film inspired by the sacrifice of Indian Army personnel. One user wrote, "A film based on Col. Santosh Babu & 19 soldiers beaten to death in Galwan and Salman’s tribute is ‘Teri sexy beauty ka fan ho gaya hu, 2 peg peeke talli ho gaya hu.’ How can anyone even think of putting a song like this in a patriotic film. He has zero respect for real martyrs." Another user commented, "Real story pe based patriotic movie me ye sab kya lyrics hai gende. Ek national hero ke character ko kiya bana diya." Another netizen expressed disappointment over the film's changing narrative and musical choices, writing in Hindi that a patriotic film's title, script and songs had seemingly undergone changes. article_sentences: The US Treasury on Wednesday imposed fresh sanctions on individuals and companies based in India and Turkiye for allegedly supporting Iran’s oil and aviation sectors respectively.
The move came a day after Democrats made large gains in the midterm elections, winning control of both houses of Congress.
The sanctions fall under “Operation Economic Outcast,” the Trump administration’s effort to choke off Iran’s oil income and the funding it provides for the conflict with the US and Israel.
“We have taken note of the sanctions,” an official in the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) told businessline.
Similar sanctions had also been imposed against Indian entities earlier this year, in August and in October.

“As we have said many times, under Operation Economic Outcast, you are either with us or against us…We know where you are, and we will sanction those who continue supporting the Iranian regime, whether by land, sea, or air,” Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent said in a Treasury statement issued on Wednesday.

Sources said there is not much that the Indian government could do about the situation as many such entities operated illegitimately and could be part of shadow fleet networks operated from cities such as Dubai.
“No legitimate Indian business imports oil from Iran.
They do not want to go against the US sanctions.
But there are shadow fleets that may be operating, often with bases in places such as Dubai, and the entities linked to these get into trouble,” a source tracking the matter explained.

In its latest operations, the US targeted the “vast criminal network” of India-based Suniel Kumar Sharma and his spouse, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid, who allegedly supported Iran’s shadow fleet through a web of maritime fraud.

“Their schemes have provided false flags and certifications to sanctioned vessels involved in transporting Iranian petroleum, including vessels operating on behalf of the Iranian military and its proxies,” the Treasury noted.

article_sentences: The Court observed that the right to speedy trial, being a fundamental right, cannot be subjected to stringent bail conditions.

The Supreme Court's two-judge bench today expressed reservations about another two-judge bench's judgment in Sukhwinder Singh (2026), which held that the right to speedy trial under Article 21 can't override the stringent statutory requirements for granting bail under Section 37 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1987 (NDPS).

In the verdict pronounced today in Sujit Das v UOI, a bench comprising Justice Ujjal Bhuyan and Justice Atul S Chandurkar expressed that the judgment in State of Punjab v Sukhwinder Singh @ Gora has become "per incuriam" in the light of the 2021 UOI v KA Najeeb judgment, wherein a three-judge bench held that violation of the right to speedy trial is a ground for constitutional Courts to grant bail even under special statutes which provide for stringent bail conditions.
The bench said: "In Sukhwinder Singh alias Gora, this Court observed that the right to speedy trial rooted in Article 21 of the Constitution is undoubtedly a precious constitutional right.

However, the bench proceeded to observe that in matters governed by special enactments such as the NDPS Act, particularly where the recovery is of commercial quantity, the said right under Article 21 must be exercised within the framework of Section 37 and cannot be pressed into service only on the ground of delay to override Section 37."

Noting this, Justice Bhuyan, who read the pronouncement, stated that while the coordinate bench comprising Justice Sanjay Karol and Justice AG Masih stated that Article 21 and Section 37 of the NDPS Act are to be read harmoniously and not placed in opposition to each other, the present bench feels that when the former is violated, the rigours of special enactments will melt down as held in Najeeb.
He said: "We have our reservations on the aforesaid observations made by the bench.
First and foremost, the rights conferred by Article 21 of the Constitution are not only constitutional rights, these are fundamental rights.
The right to life and liberty as enshrined in Article 21 are at the core of our constitutional jurisprudence.
These fundamental rights cannot be tinkered with so lightly, not even under a special statute."

Further, the bench stated that the observations in Sukhwinder run counter to numerous judgments where it has been reiterated that when there is a violation of Article 21 of the Constitution, the rigour of Section 37 of the NDPS Act or similar provisions under a special statute would have to give way.

Referring to those judgments, the bench said: "Please see Union of India versus K A Najeeb, Satender Kumar Antil, Mohd Muslim, Ankur Chadda, Vijay Singh versus Union of India, where this Court clearly held that Article 21 of the Constitution of India overrides Section 37 of the NDPS Act.

article_sentences: Activist Sharjeel Imam has moved the Supreme Court against a Delhi High Court order refusing him bail in an Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) case on the "larger conspiracy" behind the February 2020 riots in northeast Delhi.

In his plea before the top court, Mr. Imam contended that he should be granted bail as the prosecution has failed to examine witnesses and the one-year embargo imposed by the top court is about to expire.
The petition contended that the charge sheet was filed on September 25, 2020, in which 18 accused face trial and the prosecution has cited more than 900 witnesses, including 47 protected witnesses.
Mr. Imam submitted that despite spending six years and nine months as undertrial, the prosecution has failed to examine even a single witness.
The Delhi High Court on September 30 refused to grant bail to activists Umar Khalid and Mr. Imam in a case under UAPA on the "larger conspiracy" behind the February 2020 northeast Delhi riots.

Asserting that it is bound by "judicial discipline", the high court said it could not modify the Supreme Court's January 5 order asking the two accused to seek bail either on completion of protected witnesses' examination or expiry of one year, whichever is earlier.
Mr. Khalid and Mr. Imam challenged the trial court's July 4 decision rejecting their bail pleas for the third time since their arrest.
The trial court had rejected the bail applications, saying it had "no option but to follow" the Supreme Court's January 5 order and, therefore, could neither entertain the plea nor grant any relief.

The high court had noted that while denying bail to the two accused in January, the top court had said their roles were distinct from the other co-accused, and they were the "ideological drivers" of the alleged conspiracy.
Mr. Khalid and Mr. Imam have been booked under UAPA on allegations of being among the masterminds of the February 2020 riots that left 53 people dead and more than 700 injured.
The violence erupted during protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act (CAA), 2019, and the National Register of Citizens (NRC).

Activist Khalid Saifi and former AAP councillor Tahir Hussain, among others, were also booked for their alleged involvement in the larger conspiracy case, being investigated by Delhi Police's Special Cell.

stories.title: Merchants Cannot Pass On UPI Charges To Customers, MDR Necessary To Sustain UPI Ecosystem : NPCI Tells Supreme Court
stories.summary: 96% of Person to Merchant transactions would remain free, the NPCI stated.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: 96% of Person to Merchant transactions would remain free, the NPCI stated.

Defending its decision to levy charges for transactions above ₹2,000 from individuals to merchants under the revised Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) framework for Unified Payment Interface (UPI), the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) has told the Supreme Court that merchants are barred from passing on MDR charges to customers.
It has further stated that UPI application providers cannot impose platform fees or other charges for UPI payments.

“Second, non-compliance by a Payer PSP or TPAP with the NPCI Circular's directive against passing on MDR to customers constitutes a breach of the binding obligation under the SLAs to abide by all circulars, orders, directions and instructions issued by the Answering Respondent, and exposes such Payer PSP or TPAP to compliance actions which may also lead to termination of its UPI membership and facilities.

Therefore, the non-pass-through directive to the banks and UPI service providers is a mandatory and binding direction, which is enforceable through contractual mechanism in place, and is not a mere 'assurance' or a matter of policy.
Thus, apprehension that the consumers are left exposed to an indirect burden is accordingly without any foundation”, the affidavit states.

NPCI has filed a counter affidavit filed on November 3 in a petition challenging the amendment to Section 10A of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, introduced through the Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Act, 2026, the subsequent Ministry of Finance notification and the revised MDR framework announced in September.

The Supreme Court had in September 2026 sought an affidavit explaining the basis for the move to levy charges for transactions through Unified Payment Interface (UPI) above ₹2,000 from individuals to merchants.

NPCI has submitted that around 96% of person-to-merchant transactions will remain unaffected by the revised MDR, the NPCI has refuted the apprehension that the MDR charges would cause merchants to increase prices.

“The charge under the MDR is attracted only to a small fraction i.e. approximately 4%, of P2M transactions that exceed INR 2,000 and thus, a measure confined so narrowly in its incidence affords less scope for merchants to recalibrate their pricing across their entire customer base merely on account of a charge that arises only occasionally and only above a defined value.
Accordingly, the apprehension that the MDR Framework will result in quiet revision of prices is also misconceived”, the NPCI has stated.
NPCI has stated that person-to-person transactions and transactions involving small merchants under the P2PM category will continue to remain free.

stories.headline: Supreme Court says 24-hour arrest deadline begins when person is detained
stories.title: Supreme Court says 24-hour arrest deadline begins when person is detained
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court has ruled that the 24-hour deadline for producing an arrested person before a magistrate begins from the moment their liberty is curtailed, and not from the time the police formally record the arrest.
A bench of Justices Ujjal Bhuyan and Atul S Chandurkar held that excluding the period of detention before a formal arrest from the 24-hour deadline would violate Article 22(2) of the Constitution.
The ruling came in appeals filed by four people challenging the Tripura High Court's rejection of their bail pleas in a case under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act.
The four accused were detained on September 29, 2025, at around 2 pm during a search and seizure operation.
However, the police formally recorded their arrest only at 11 am the following day.
The Supreme Court held that they should have been produced before a magistrate within 24 hours of their detention on September 29.
According to a LiveLaw report, the court found that the accused had been kept in custody for around 18 hours without judicial oversight, violating their constitutional rights.
It consequently ordered their immediate release.
"Article 22(2) does not sanction exclusion of the time taken for inquiry or investigation before the arresting authority could effect arrest of the detainee," the bench observed.
The court clarified that the only period that can be excluded while calculating the 24-hour deadline is the time required to travel from the place of arrest to the magistrate's court.
It rejected the argument that detention before a formal arrest should be treated differently, observing that fundamental rights cannot be temporarily suspended during an investigation.

The bench also disapproved of earlier rulings by the Orissa High Court in Aryaman Pattanaik, the Kerala High Court in Arun K Thomas and the Madras High Court in Kannan, which had allowed pre-arrest detention to be excluded from the 24-hour calculation.
